sources.citation: Mutonya, Mungai & Timothy H. Parsons. 2004. KiKAR: a Swahili variety in Kenya's colonial army. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 25(2): 111-125. doi:10.1515/jall.2004.25.2.111
sources.note: Nothing. Read in full (15 pp.); a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|tone|penult|syllab|prosod finds only 'accentuated' (p. 124, non-technical). Section 5 'A linguistic sketch of KiKAR' (pp. 119-124) covers noun-class reduction, morphophonemic simplification (nasal assimilation dropped), omission/substitution, and lexicon. Only sound remarks: Newell's ms. has 'grammar notes (pp. 4-12) on vowel pronunciation' (p. 118); speakers 'simplified Swahili grammar, sound and lexical structures' (p. 119); English loans restructured 'to conform to the vowel-ending structure of Bantu words' (p. 123…
